stories.title: AI Boom, Affordability Drive Rent Gains in a Handful of Apartment Markets
stories.excerpt: Even as September marked the 38th consecutive month of annual declines nationwide in apartment rents, two market cohorts are seeing rent gains, Realtor.com reported. The AI boom is spiking demand in the Bay Area, while affordably priced metro areas are reversing their annual declines. The strongest rent growth is in the Bay Area, where the AI boom is drawing young professionals seeking employment opportunities. Median asking rent in San Jose rose 6.0% year over year to a new high of $3,565, while San Francisco rent increased 4.8% to $3,057, just $48 below its summer 2022 pandemic peak. Elsewhere in the U.S., markets such as St. Louis, Minneapolis, Virginia Beach, Riverside and Las Vegas have shifted from rent price declines to price gains as renters seek more affordable options outside nearby high-cost markets. Both St. Louis and Minneapolis have drawn renters from Chicago, according to Realtor.com. Nationally, the median asking rent fell 0.4% year-over-year, the slowest annual decline in three years. The post AI Boom, Affordability Drive Rent Gains in a Handful of Apartment Markets appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Bay Area rents rising: San Jose up 6.0% YoY to $3,565; SF up 4.8% to $3,057.
Affordability-driven reversals: St. Louis, Minneapolis, Vegas shift from declines to gains; drawing renters from high-cost metros.
National slowdown easing: median asking rent down 0.4% YoY, slowest decline in three years.
stories.summary: Two distinct demand cohorts are reversing the 38-month national rent decline. The Bay Area—driven by AI hiring—posted its strongest growth with San Jose and San Francisco rents near or exceeding pandemic peaks. Simultaneously, affordable metros including St. Louis, Minneapolis, and Las Vegas have shifted to year-over-year gains as renters flee expensive neighboring markets like Chicago. Nationally, the pace of rent erosion has slowed to just 0.4% annual decline, the least severe in three years.
stories.impact: Bay Area (SF/San Jose) represents a genuine reopening of high-end development opportunity on AI-fueled employer demand and talent migration; undersupply in those markets will support rents and development yields. Conversely, migration into affordable secondary markets (St. Louis, Minneapolis, Vegas) signals demand shift away from expensive coastal metros—a long-term headwind for high-cost markets and tailwind for secondary-market supply. Developers should prioritize Bay Area acquisitions before AI-driven rents fully capitalize and shift capital to secondary markets experiencing inbound migration.

stories.title: Greystar Opens New 416-Unit Community North of Boston
stories.excerpt: Greystar has begun to welcome residents to Juniper, its fifth apartment community in a formerly industrial neighborhood that the company is redeveloping north of Boston in Everett, MA. The 416-unit property at 201 Mill Road marks the final community delivered as part of Greystar’s $880 million transformation of Everett’s Commercial Triangle Economic Development District, creating a connected neighborhood featuring 1,905 new apartment homes, 6,500 square feet of retail space, and community green space and parks. The new property features apartments ranging from one to three bedrooms and more than 15,000 square feet of amenity space, including a gym and community pet spa. Juniper’s offerings also include a pickleball court, bocce court, nine-hole mini golf course, and dog park. Greystar, the largest apartment operator in the U.S., broke ground on the property in the summer of 2024 and topped off construction in December of last year. Image courtesy of Greystar. The post Greystar Opens New 416-Unit Community North of Boston appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Greystar delivered 416-unit Juniper north of Boston, final phase of $880M Everett redevelopment.
Commercial Triangle district now includes 1,905 total units, 6,500 SF retail, green space across five communities.
Project demonstrates large-scale master-planning and industrial-to-residential conversion in tight Boston submarket.
stories.summary: Greystar completed Juniper, a 416-unit apartment community in Everett, Massachusetts, marking the final delivery of its $880 million transformation of the Commercial Triangle Economic Development District. The five-property, 1,905-unit development adds significant housing stock to a formerly industrial area north of Boston with retail and public amenities. The project was ground-broken in summer 2024 and topped off in December 2024, reflecting accelerated execution in a constrained market.
stories.impact: Boston North/Everett submarket now absorbed 1,905 units from a single sponsor over a concentrated period, signaling both strong execution and potential supply saturation risk in that immediate submarket. Greystar's completion validates urban infill/brownfield redevelopment model at scale but also tightens available land in the Boston North corridor; developers should prioritize competing deals in secondary Boston rings (Somerville, Cambridge, Quincy) before Everett landlocked by Greystar's footprint.

stories.title: AT&T Reveals Construction Schedule of $1.3B Plano Campus
stories.excerpt: Construction of the new AT&T headquarters planned in Plano is expected to begin in December. The $1.3 billion campus will include numerous buildings ranging in size from 225,000 to 680,000 square feet, making up over 2.3 million square feet of office space. The facility will include over 2.5 million square feet for parking garages. The project is expected to be under construction through 2029. KDC is developing the project. The city approved a $20 million economic incentive for the headquarters. AT&T will be required to meet employment benchmarks in exchange for the incentive. The facility is expected to bring 10,000 jobs to the region by 2039. The future headquarters of AT&T was the former Electronic Data Systems (EDS) campus site. Demolition of Ross Perot’s former EDS campus is still ongoing at the 54-acre site along Legacy Drive and Parkwood Boulevard. The post AT&T Reveals Construction Schedule of $1.3B Plano Campus appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: AT&T $1.3B Plano HQ: 2.3M SF office, construction Dec. 2025–2029, targets 10,000 jobs by 2039.
City of Plano approved $20M incentive; AT&T subject to employment benchmarks on former EDS campus.
Demolition ongoing on 54-acre site; KDC developing; phased delivery through end of decade.
stories.summary: AT&T announced a $1.3 billion headquarters campus in Plano, Texas, with construction beginning December 2025 and running through 2029. The project will deliver 2.3 million square feet of office space and create 10,000 jobs by 2039. The city provided $20 million in incentives contingent on employment targets. The development sits on the 54-acre former EDS campus, with demolition currently underway.
stories.impact: Dallas-Fort Worth/Plano: This represents a major employer commitment and multi-year construction activity signaling confidence in the market. The phased delivery (2025–2029) means sustained job growth will compound over years, driving inbound migration and household formation well into 2030s. Multifamily developers should acquire land in concentric rings around Plano immediately—the 10,000-job pipeline will create lagged demand for apartments 6–24 months after workers arrive. Timing now to deliver Class A and workforce product by 2027–2028 to capture first waves of AT&T talent and supporting services workforce.

stories.title: As Investors Pull Back, L.A. Warehouse Users Step In
stories.excerpt: While the logistics and shipping sectors seem more uncertain than they have in years, with shifting tariffs and trade policy compounded by a diesel fuel crisis, a number of companies are looking to invest in a more stable future. Increasingly, that means owning, not renting. It’s a dynamic that’s playing out more and more in Southern California, the nation’s largest industrial market. Industrial users “competed actively” with investors across Southern California early this year, according to data from Smith Industrial Partners, with buyers paying a measurable premium to own rather than lease, a “signal that long-term confidence in the asset class remains intact.” Smith found that renters looking to buy have constantly outpaid institutional buyers, seeking to lock-in current occupancy costs. And, after trading in vacant warehouses across the region increased last year, eating into some of the post-pandemic glut, sales volumes have continued to rise. The push for deals that turn operators into owners comes from a variety of overlapping trends, said Erik Hanson, a senior director of capital markets for JLL based in San Francisco. First, on a national level, companies have the dry powder, and after quarters of solid profits, they’re more efficient, and have strong balance sheets and the ability to deploy that capital. At the same time, the choppiness of the market, exacerbated by recent interest rate increases, is signaling to traditional institutional players that it’s time to pull back. That’s opening the lane for a different class of buyer. “It all gives owner-users more leverage to win and buy their real estate,” said Hanson. At a time when companies are more worried than ever about disruptions, buying key warehouse locations to guarantee resilience and continuity seems like a smart business move, said Zac Rogers, associate professor of operations and supply chain management at Colorado State University. bullets: L.A. industrial users outbidding investors for ownership; renters paying premium to lock occupancy costs.
Vacant warehouse turnover in Southern California increased last year, reducing post-pandemic glut.
Tariff and fuel uncertainty driving operator-to-owner conversion trend; long-term asset confidence intact.
stories.summary: In Southern California, the nation's largest industrial market, warehouse users are increasingly buying rather than leasing, paying measurable premiums to institutional investors to secure long-term occupancy. According to Smith Industrial Partners, this shift reflects uncertainty around tariffs, trade policy, and diesel fuel costs, combined with operators' desire to lock in current occupancy costs. Vacant warehouse absorption has continued despite rising sales volumes, suggesting ongoing supply tightening.
stories.impact: Los Angeles industrial: The user-buyer premium signals supply tightness and operational anxiety around future cost inflation—occupants believe owning is cheaper than future-market leasing. While this shifts capital away from investor purchases (negative for stabilized-asset pricing), it reveals that multifamily developers focused on industrial-adjacent properties or logistics-hub submarkets should expect higher land competition and pricing. Additionally, tariff volatility may reduce import volumes and e-commerce last-mile demand, softening long-term warehouse absorption in L.A.—timing matters for industrial conversion projects.

stories.title: Ascension Seton Acquires Three Austin-Area Medical Facilities
stories.excerpt: Ascension Seton acquired three Texas health care facilities from Family Hospital Systems. The healthcare centers are located in Round Rock, Cedar Park and near Lake Travis. The healthcare system stated the move is planned to expand emergency care access amid growth in the greater Austin area. Family Hospital at Lake Travis (shown), Family Medical Center at Lakeline, and Family Medical Center at Round Rock will officially come under the ownership of Ascension Seton later this year, once the deal closes. There should be no disruptions to care during the transition. Before the sale, Family Hospital Systems owned 7 properties in Texas. After the sale goes through, Family Hospital will still own the Emergency Room at Cedar Park, the Emergency Room at Georgetown, the Hospital at Bandera and the Hospital at Brushy Creek The post Ascension Seton Acquires Three Austin-Area Medical Facilities appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Ascension Seton acquired three Texas healthcare facilities: Round Rock, Cedar Park, Lake Travis.
Move aims to expand emergency care access amid greater Austin area growth.
Family Hospital Systems retains 4 properties post-sale.
stories.summary: Ascension Seton acquired three healthcare facilities in the Austin metropolitan area—Family Hospital at Lake Travis, Family Medical Center at Lakeline (Cedar Park), and Family Medical Center at Round Rock—from Family Hospital Systems. The healthcare system stated the acquisitions are designed to expand emergency care capacity and access in response to population growth in greater Austin. The deal closes later in 2025.
stories.impact: Austin: Healthcare infrastructure expansion signals confidence in continued population and household growth in the metro. Ascension's capital deployment into emergency-care expansion typically precedes sustained physician and healthcare-worker recruitment, creating secondary demand for service-sector and professional housing. Multifamily developers should tag secondary corridors (Round Rock, Cedar Park) as emerging demand nodes; healthcare employment tends to drive white-collar household formation 12–24 months after facility expansion. However, impact is modest relative to office or tech employer anchors.

stories.title: Baron Picks Up 7-Property SW USA Warehouse Portfolio
stories.excerpt: Piercey Realty Ventures has spun off a seven-property industrial portfolio with assets in Phoenix and one in Las Vegas. The portfolio totaled 426,000 square feet. Baron Properties was the buyer. Commercial Edge reports that the assets feature flexible configurations geared toward small- to mid-bay users and infill locations with access to regional freight corridors. The portfolio is fully leased. Its tenant roster includes a mix of 11 regional and national occupiers. The largest of the Arizona properties is 1020-1030 East University Drive, which measures 104,876 square feet on 5.26 acres. Cushman & Wakefield’s team of Will Strong, Molly Miller, Jack Stamets, Michael Matchett and Madeline Warren arranged the transaction and represented both the buyer and seller. Piercey Realty Ventures was also represented by Lee & Associates’ Phoenix team of Ken McQueen, Chris McClurg, Blake Peters and Jack Sims, as well as Cushman & Wakefield’s Jason Griffis and Alma Cuevas in Nevada. The post Baron Picks Up 7-Property SW USA Warehouse Portfolio appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Baron Properties acquired 7-property, 426K SF industrial portfolio from Piercey Realty Ventures.
Assets span Phoenix and Las Vegas; fully leased to 11 regional/national tenants.
Largest property: 104,876 SF at 1020-1030 East University Drive, Phoenix; infill, small-to-mid-bay configurations.
stories.summary: Baron Properties purchased a seven-property industrial portfolio totaling 426,000 square feet across Phoenix and Las Vegas from Piercey Realty Ventures. The fully leased assets feature flexible, small-to-mid-bay configurations in infill locations with access to regional freight corridors. The largest property is 104,876 square feet on 5.26 acres in Phoenix. Cushman & Wakefield and Lee & Associates brokered the transaction.
stories.impact: Phoenix/Las Vegas: This portfolio acquisition reinforces investor appetite for stabilized, fully leased industrial assets in southwestern markets despite macro uncertainty. The small-to-mid-bay, infill focus suggests demand from fragmented user base (e-commerce, regional distribution, light manufacturing). Limited relevance to multifamily unless developer is considering industrial-conversion or mixed-use development in Phoenix—in which case land competition in Phoenix infill is high and appreciation likely ahead of conversion.

stories.title: S3 Capital Lends $53M for Upper East Side Condo Tower
stories.excerpt: A joint venture between Grand Cru Real Estate (GCRE) and Visabe has sealed $52.5 million of construction financing to develop a condominium building on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, Commercial Observer has learned. S3 Capital originated the loan to facilitate the sponsorship’s 28-unit condo project at 1527 York Avenue. Located on the corner of York Avenue and East 81st Street, the 20-story tower will have condo units that range from one to five bedrooms. Resident amenities will include a full-time doorman, fitness center, recreation lounge and children’s playroom. “Upper East Side condo buyers are a specific audience, and a 28-unit building with layouts up to five bedrooms is aimed squarely at them,” Shawn Safdie, head of origination at S3 Capital, said in a statement. “GCRE understands that buyer, and their successful execution on a recent project gave us the confidence to partner with them again.” Oak CM will serve as construction manager and general contractor. Construction is slated to begin in early 2027. Steven Jemal, senior managing director of origination at S3, noted that it also financed a condo project for GCRE at 439 East 77th Street four blocks south of this latest project. “We know GCRE well from 439 East 77th Street, so we were comfortable with the team and the submarket from the start,” Jemal said in a statement. Salomon Cojab, principal of GCRE, noted that the development is growing with Jack Cattan and Robert Salame also principals. “This is a very exciting opportunity for both GCRE and Visabe to expand their Upper East Side footprint following the development of 439 East 77th Street,” Cojab said in a statement. “We continue to show our belief in and commitment to the neighborhood by providing new quality residences that we hope people will call their forever homes.” Visabe did not immediately return a request for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: S3 Capital originated $52.5M construction loan for 28-unit condo tower, 1527 York Avenue, Manhattan.
Upper East Side project: 20 stories, 1–5 bedroom units, construction begins early 2027.
Joint venture Grand Cru Real Estate and Visabe; full-service luxury amenities; Oak CM as GC.
stories.summary: A joint venture between Grand Cru Real Estate and Visabe secured $52.5 million in construction financing from S3 Capital for a 28-unit condominium tower at 1527 York Avenue on the Upper East Side. The 20-story building will range from one to five bedrooms and include luxury amenities. Construction is scheduled to begin in early 2027, with Oak CM serving as general contractor.
stories.impact: Manhattan/Upper East Side: Condo development is largely outside multifamily rental focus, but the deal signals continued capital availability for residential development in prime Manhattan and sponsor confidence in high-end ownership demand. Modest relevance to multifamily developers unless considering stabilized-rental-to-condo conversion strategies; construction financing at $52.5M for 28 units implies ~$1.9M per unit hard cost, reflecting Manhattan's cost structure.

stories.title: Camera Brand Fujifilm Takes 13K SF at 210 Lafayette Street in SoHo
stories.excerpt: A Japanese camera manufacturer is setting up shop in Manhattan’s photogenic SoHo neighborhood. Fujifilm signed a lease for 12,700 square feet at Comjem Associates’ 210 Lafayette Street for what could be a brick-and-mortar retail location similar to stores operated by B&H or Adorama. Not much else is known about the deal, but Fujifilm’s new space between Kenmare and Spring streets will span three levels, the New York Post reported. The space has been largely vacant in recent years, despite popular retail neighbors such as Eataly SoHo. Cushman & Wakefield’s Andrew Kahn and Matt Weinreb represented both sides of the deal. C&W, however, declined to comment. Comjem Associates did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “We’re building something big,” a Fujifilm spokesperson said in a statement. “Details will be shared as soon as they’re available.” The transaction closed as SoHo retail leasing continued its upward trajectory with average asking rents in the submarket ranging between $896 and $1,409 per square foot, depending on the specific corridor, according to a third-quarter retail report from CBRE. SoHo, one of the hottest retail markets in North America, has asking rents well above the Manhattan average of $707 per square foot, which grew 5 percent on a year-over-year basis in the third quarter, the CBRE report said. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Fujifilm signed 12,700 SF lease at 210 Lafayette Street, SoHo, spanning three levels.
Likely brick-and-mortar retail/experience center; space previously vacant despite neighborhood strength.
SoHo retail leasing accelerating; average asking rents rising; Cushman & Wakefield brokered deal.
stories.summary: Fujifilm leased 12,700 square feet across three levels at 210 Lafayette Street in SoHo, likely for a flagship retail location similar to B&H or Adorama. The space had remained largely vacant despite strong retail neighbors including Eataly. Cushman & Wakefield represented both parties. SoHo retail leasing has shown upward momentum with rising asking rents.
stories.impact: Manhattan/SoHo: Minimal direct impact to multifamily development. Fujifilm's signature retail commitment signals neighborhood vitality and retail absorption acceleration in SoHo; as retail rents rise and retail real estate tightens, landlords may accelerate residential-use conversion or mixed-use development in secondary SoHo properties, potentially competing for development capital.

stories.title: ICBC Supplies $24.4M Refi for 16-Story NoMad Office Tower
stories.excerpt: LMR Assets, a real estate investment entity of Gourmet Home Products, landed a $24.4 million loan to refinance its office and retail tower at 148 Madison Avenue, Commercial Observer has learned. The U.S. arm of Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) supplied the loan for the 16-story building. The circa-1917 tower, located in Manhattan’s NoMad neighborhood, occupies a full Madison Avenue block face between East 31st and East 32nd streets. Meridian Capital Group’s Benjamin Klugmann and Ariel Taieb arranged the deal for LMR. “ICBC recognized the quality of the real estate and the strength of the sponsorship, and we were pleased to deliver a financing structure that fits the property and the owners’ long-term plans for the building,” Klugmann said in a statement to CO. The sponsor, led by Jack Saadeh, Victor Saadeh and Jack Yadid, acquired the building for $31.3 million in June 2024 in an owner-occupier deal. It was the first commercial real estate purchase for the real estate arm of Gourmet Home Products, which owns and operates several houseware and lifestyle brands. The company moved its operations there from its previous home at 347 Fifth Avenue. Since its purchase, LMR has invested in capital improvements across the 71,871-square-foot tower, according to Meridian. The property features 15 office spaces and a retail space currently occupied by Brazilian luxury furniture brand Ornare. Spokespeople for Gourmet Home Products and ICBC did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: ICBC (China) supplied $24.4M refi for 148 Madison Avenue, NoMad, 16-story office/retail tower.
Sponsor LMR Assets (Gourmet Home Products real estate arm) acquired property June 2024 for $31.3M.
Circa-1917 building; full Madison Avenue block face; first CRE purchase by sponsor's real estate entity.
stories.summary: Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) originated a $24.4 million refinance loan for LMR Assets' 148 Madison Avenue, a 16-story office and retail tower in Manhattan's NoMad neighborhood. The sponsor, led by a real estate arm of Gourmet Home Products, acquired the property in June 2024 for $31.3 million in an owner-occupier transaction and has now refinanced to support long-term ownership plans.
stories.impact: Manhattan/NoMad: ICBC's willingness to refinance Manhattan office suggests foreign capital still active in stabilized U.S. real estate despite macro headwinds. However, office is cyclically challenged and NoMad's retail/office mix in an aging building presents conversion risk. Minimal direct multifamily relevance unless NoMad sees office-to-residential conversion wave—timing and zoning make conversion unlikely in near term but worth monitoring if NoMad office rents compress further.

stories.title: The New York Housing Court Problem Comes Home to City Hall
stories.excerpt: There is an irony in watching New York City government confront the time and cost of a housing dispute from the property owner’s side. One of the city’s largest residential property owners is confronting the same fundamental question owners of privately held buildings do: What good is a property right if exercising it takes years? At New York City Housing Authority’s (NYCHA) Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea campuses, the city wants to replace 2,056 aging apartments and add thousands of new homes. The redevelopment is expected to leverage private capital and transform public housing in a desirable neighborhood. But redevelopment requires possession. Residents challenged the redevelopment, and NYCHA is now confronting holdouts. Ben Tapper. Photo: Courtesy of Lee & Associates The details are familiar to multifamily owners in New York City. An owner has a redevelopment plan, project schedule, financing commitments and economic rationale for moving forward. But some occupants won’t leave. The government is now experiencing this same problem … and the lesson is bigger than Chelsea. The city Housing Court has become an economic variable in the value of real estate. That should concern everyone. Developers cannot demolish buildings they don’t fully control. Contractors cannot work around indefinite occupancy. Construction financing does not pause because a project is delayed. The fundamental reality of economics is that every week a development sits in limbo carries costs. The city is now discovering this firsthand. The irony is particularly striking because New York has spent years telling private owners the city’s housing shortage demands more investment, more construction and more apartments. Yet the same government attempting to accelerate housing production is confronting a system in which obtaining possession is a lengthy legal exercise. bullets: NYC Housing Court delays plague NYCHA's Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea redevelopment; 2,056 units slated for replacement.
NYCHA confronting holdout tenants; project dependent on possession but court backlogs extending timelines.
Issue extends beyond Chelsea: Housing Court dysfunction raising redevelopment cost and risk citywide.
stories.summary: New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) is confronting lengthy Housing Court delays in its effort to secure possession of the Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea public housing campuses for a planned redevelopment that would replace 2,056 aging apartments and add thousands of new units. Resident challenges and holdouts are stalling the project despite financing commitments and clear economic rationale. The situation mirrors private-owner struggles with Housing Court backlogs, highlighting systemic delays in the city's judicial capacity.
stories.impact: New York City/Manhattan: Housing Court dysfunction is a material risk to multifamily development economics citywide. Any redevelopment or conversion requiring tenant displacement or possession faces unpredictable legal timelines, inflating soft costs, extending carry periods, and compressing returns. Multifamily developers should model 18–36 month possession delays into any NYC project requiring relocation; this shifts economics toward new-ground-up or already-vacant properties and raises the bar for value-add conversions. NYCHA's public struggle may prompt municipal reform, but near-term risk remains elevated for possession-dependent deals.
